title: The Real Problem Underlying India-China Tensions | NOEMA
gist: Journalist Pallavi Aiyar argues India-China tension is driven less by the border dispute or the growing economic gap than by a decades-old communication failure: China still filters India through a colonial-era 'subordinate' stereotype ('Ah San'), India filters China through the 1962 war's 'betrayal' narrative, and both narratives are reinforced by the near-total absence of resident foreign correspondents on either side.

themes.theme: Power Asymmetry Between India and China

insights.claim: India and China had similar per-capita incomes as recently as 1990, but by 2025 China's GDP of $19.4 trillion was nearly five times India's $4.1 trillion.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: The economic gap has widened so far since parity in 1990 that China now negotiates from a position of overwhelming leverage in any bilateral trade, investment or border settlement with India.
insights.quote: By 2025, China’s GDP of $19.4 trillion was nearly five times larger than India’s $4.1 trillion.
insights.locator: As recently as 1990, India and China had similar per capita incomes

insights.claim: China views the United States as the only country with real strategic leverage over it, treating India as part of a supporting cast, whereas China occupies a dominant, constant place in India's military procurement and border-infrastructure calculations.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Investors modeling India-China de-escalation should note the relationship is structurally asymmetric: China has far less incentive than India to prioritize the bilateral relationship, which limits how far any reset can go.
insights.locator: India and China do not think about each other with equivalent intensity

insights.claim: At a spring 2026 Beijing dialogue organized by the Center for China and Globalization, a Chinese participant told the visiting Indian journalist delegation that India should accept its relative economic weakness and leverage Chinese strength for its own development; the Indian delegation reacted with visible offense.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Shows that even technocratic, well-intentioned reset dialogues can misfire on tone, signaling that official India-China thaw efforts remain fragile and slow to translate into durable policy change.
insights.locator: At the meeting I attended in Beijing, one of the Chinese participants was blunt

themes.theme: Colonial-Era Legacy: The 'Ah San' Perception of India

insights.claim: From 1885 to the early 1940s, Sikh policemen recruited from Punjab made up about 12% of the Shanghai Municipal Police under British colonial rule; Shanghainese nicknamed them 'hong tou Ah San' ('red-headed number three'), embedding the idea of Indians as subordinate colonial enforcers in Chinese popular memory.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: This 140-year-old ethnic slur still shapes how Chinese social media and officials frame India's foreign-policy choices today, a durable cultural headwind that formal diplomacy alone cannot dissolve.
insights.quote: The Shanghainese called the Sikhs hong tou Ah San — literally “red-headed number three.”
insights.locator: In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Sikhs were among the most recognizable symbols

insights.claim: Parsi and Marwari merchants were key commercial intermediaries in the British-forced opium trade into Qing China; Parsi traders in Canton's foreign enclave outnumbered English merchants 41 to 32 in 1831, widening to 52 versus 35 by 1835.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Illustrates a historical precedent where Indian commercial actors profited as intermediaries in a coercive China trade relationship — a memory China's public still associates with Indian business dealings today.
insights.quote: By 1831, there were 41 Parsis in Canton’s foreign enclave, outnumbering the 32 English merchants
insights.locator: Indian traders, too, had their role in the colonial economy of China’s humiliation

insights.claim: Some of the same Marwari commercial capital accumulated through opium speculation — including the fortune of Shivnarain Birla, grandfather of G.D. Birla, a close associate of Gandhi — later helped fund the Indian independence movement.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: A little-known historical irony: capital tied to China's opium devastation indirectly financed India's own anti-colonial movement, complicating simple victim/perpetrator framings each country uses about the other.
insights.locator: A little-known fact in India is that some of the same commercial capital

insights.claim: China reads India's Quad membership, US defense ties, and pursuit of closer EU trade relations not as sovereign strategic choices but as a modern continuation of the Ah San role — India again serving Western interests against China.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Any Indian move toward deeper Western security or trade integration (Quad, EU FTA talks) is likely to be read in Beijing as provocation rather than neutral hedging, raising the odds of retaliatory friction (border pressure, trade curbs) around those announcements.
insights.locator: A significant strand of Chinese opinion still seems to view India’s international positioning

insights.claim: When President George W. Bush secured India a 2008 Nuclear Suppliers Group waiver for civilian nuclear trade despite India not signing the Non-Proliferation Treaty, Beijing interpreted it not as recognition of India's strategic weight but as confirmation India had become a favored American client.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Precedent suggests future US-India strategic or technology agreements (e.g., defense co-production, semiconductor deals) will likely be read by Beijing through the same distrustful lens, informing China's response calculus.
insights.locator: When President George W. Bush secured India a waiver at the Nuclear Suppliers Group in 2008

insights.claim: In 1954 India and China signed the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence, and Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru invested heavily in a vision of the two countries jointly leading a non-aligned, post-colonial world order.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: The scale of Nehru's earlier idealism is the baseline against which 1962 registered as an especially deep betrayal in Indian collective memory, a psychological anchor that still colors India's China policy.
insights.locator: In 1954, the two countries signed the Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence

insights.claim: In October 1962 China launched simultaneous attacks on India in Aksai Chin and the North-East Frontier Agency (now Arunachal Pradesh); Indian forces, hugely outnumbered and unprepared, collapsed, and the war ended in late November with a unilateral Chinese ceasefire after its objectives were met.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: The decisive, one-sided nature of the 1962 defeat is why India still treats any Chinese military move near the border as an existential-risk signal, keeping Indian defense budgets and border infrastructure spending on a permanent upward trajectory.
insights.locator: But in October 1962, China launched simultaneous attacks against India

insights.claim: China's official account frames 1962 not as unprovoked aggression but as a 'self-defense counterattack' responding to Indian military encroachment into disputed territory, sharpened by suspicion after the Dalai Lama's 1959 flight to India that New Delhi sought to separate Tibet from Chinese control.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: China's Tibet-security framing means any perceived Indian gesture toward the Tibetan exile community carries outsized risk of triggering a disproportionate Chinese security response.
insights.quote: not unprovoked aggression but a “self-defense counterattack” in response to Indian military encroachment into disputed territory
insights.locator: The Chinese have their own account of 1962

insights.claim: Indian schools do not teach that China's 1962 attack followed months of Indian troops establishing forward posts along the contested border; instead Indian education emphasizes Nehru's misplaced faith that war was unthinkable and China's betrayal of post-colonial solidarity.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: A one-sided national narrative on either side reduces the domestic political space for Indian leaders to pursue compromise with China without being accused of weakness, constraining diplomatic flexibility.
insights.locator: That China’s attack came after months of Indian troops establishing forward posts

insights.claim: China's arming of Pakistan, visibly demonstrated when Chinese-built J-10C fighters were deployed against Indian aircraft in aerial battles in May 2025, is interpreted in India not as routine alliance politics but as a deliberate strategy of encirclement timed to coincide with India's vulnerable moments.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: China-Pakistan military technology transfers (like the J-10C) are a concrete, trackable signal of escalation risk on the India-Pakistan border that has direct implications for regional risk premia and Indian defense procurement decisions.
insights.locator: China’s arming of Pakistan — visibly demonstrated when Chinese-built J-10C fighters

themes.theme: Collapse of Resident Journalism Deepens the Information Gap

insights.claim: Between 2016 and 2023, tit-for-tat expulsions left India and China with almost no resident foreign correspondents from each other's country; by 2024, when the current bilateral thaw began, there was only one Indian journalist (Press Trust of India) based in China and no Chinese journalists in India at all.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: The near-total loss of first-hand journalistic coverage is a leading indicator of how badly bilateral relations deteriorated post-2020, and its slow reversal is a concrete, trackable proxy for measuring the depth of any real thaw.
insights.quote: there was only a single Indian journalist for the Press Trust of India based in China, and no Chinese journalists in India at all
insights.locator: Between 2016 and 2023, a series of tit-for-tat exchanges

insights.claim: Since 2024, one additional Indian correspondent has joined the Beijing-based foreign press corps, and a single Xinhua correspondent is expected to be posted to New Delhi shortly.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Journalist-visa reciprocity is a low-cost, high-signal metric investors and analysts can monitor as an early indicator of genuine India-China diplomatic normalization, ahead of harder economic or border commitments.
insights.locator: In the intervening months, one more Indian correspondent has been added

insights.claim: With resident correspondents largely absent, online trolls and self-styled nationalist commentators ('professors from WhatsApp University') have filled the information gap, generating reality-distorting hyper-nationalism and xenophobia on both sides.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Social-media-driven nationalism is harder to walk back than diplomatic statements, meaning public opinion may lag or actively constrain any official India-China rapprochement even after government-level tensions ease.
insights.locator: In their place, we get online trolls and professors from WhatsApp University

insights.claim: India and China, which together comprise a third of the world's population and share a 4,000-kilometer border, still get most of their information about each other from third-party, usually Western, sources rather than direct reporting.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Reliance on Western intermediary framing distorts how both giant economies perceive each other's risk and opportunity, which can produce mispriced geopolitical risk in markets that depend on accurate bilateral-relations signals.
insights.locator: These are nuclear-armed neighbors that together comprise a third of the world’s population

themes.theme: Divergent Perceptual Lenses Between the Two Countries

insights.claim: The author argues that, per communication theory, the fix for persistent India-China miscommunication is not to state positions more forcefully but to learn the other side's implicit assumptions and the unstated context behind their words.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Suggests diplomatic and business engagement strategies that invest in cultural fluency (not just louder lobbying or transactional deals) will outperform in reducing friction with Chinese counterparts over time.
insights.quote: the solution to persistent miscommunication is not to speak louder. It is to learn the other’s language
insights.locator: In communication theory, the solution to persistent miscommunication

insights.claim: As an Indian correspondent in Beijing, the author noticed she read the same scenes differently than Western colleagues — for example, seeing 'discipline' in Beijing's third ring road traffic where Western reporters saw 'chaos' — because her own cultural 'normal' was closer to China's than the West's.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Indicates that India-origin analysts or investors covering China may pick up on social and economic signals that Western-trained observers miss (or over-flag), a potential edge case for differentiated China research.
insights.quote: Where they saw chaos, say while looking at the traffic on a typical afternoon on Beijing’s third ring road, I saw discipline
insights.locator: Where they saw chaos, say while looking at the traffic

insights.claim: India regards itself as China's civilizational peer and creditor because Buddhism, which shaped Chinese culture, philosophy, art and governance for two millennia, originated in India — a status China's contemporary strategic posture toward India does not reflect.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: This civilizational self-image is a source of Indian resistance to Chinese economic and diplomatic pressure, meaning Beijing's leverage from raw GDP size may translate less smoothly into political deference than the numbers alone suggest.
insights.locator: India stands toe-to-toe with China as a civilizational peer

themes.theme: Outlook: Nationalism Limits How Far a Fix Can Go

insights.claim: Both India and China are currently in the grip of an overheated nationalism that domestic political actors have weaponized to distract from internal troubles, a dynamic the author says bringing back journalists cannot by itself erase.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Investors should treat any India-China diplomatic thaw as capped by domestic political incentives on both sides, limiting the durability of de-escalation trades (e.g., border-tension risk premia) even amid positive headlines.
insights.locator: Both countries are in the throes of an overheated nationalism

insights.claim: The author's central thesis is that restoring resident foreign correspondents in both countries is a necessary but insufficient first step; only sustained, direct, multi-year contact between the two societies can begin to close the historical and communication gaps distorting bilateral dialogue.
insights.speaker: PALLAVI AIYAR
insights.so_what: Frames journalist-access normalization as a leading, monitorable milestone on the path to deeper India-China economic and diplomatic re-engagement, useful for tracking the pace of any relationship reset.
insights.locator: Bringing back journalists will not erase India and China’s protracted history
